title: The US Federal Reserve responds to the rise in oil prices | Wood Mackenzie
gist: The Fed hiked to 3.75-4% specifically to stop a 40% gasoline / 76% diesel price surge from broadening into general inflation, while Wood Mackenzie forecasts Brent reaching US$125/bbl in October. The bigger risk it flags is second-order: with up to two-thirds of 2026 US GDP growth driven by AI capex, higher rates plus a fuel-cost squeeze on consumers could deflate the AI investment boom and tip the US into recession.

themes.theme: Fed reaction function to energy shock

insights.claim: The US Federal Reserve raised the federal funds target rate by a quarter point to 3.75-4%, with fuel prices a key factor in the decision.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Rate policy is now explicitly energy-reactive; further oil upside raises the odds of additional hikes rather than cuts, repricing the whole front end.
insights.quote: When the US Federal Reserve raised the federal funds target interest rate last week, by a quarter point to 3.75-4%, fuel prices were a key factor in the decision.
insights.locator: When the US Federal Reserve raised

insights.claim: Fed chairman Kevin Warsh framed the central bank's job as preventing relative price changes in oil and food from broadening out, explicitly disclaiming any ability to affect individual prices.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: This reaction function means the Fed tightens into supply shocks rather than looking through them — a hawkish regime for rate-sensitive assets.
insights.quote: “We cannot affect any individual price, whether it be oil prices, whether it be foodstuffs at the grocery store,” said Fed chairman Kevin Warsh after the decision was announced.

insights.claim: A healthy underlying economy — roughly 2.3% GDP growth this year and 4.1% unemployment — is precisely what makes the Fed fear pass-through, because businesses in tight conditions can protect margins by passing fuel costs to consumers.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Strong labour data is now hawkish, not dovish: good macro prints increase, not decrease, the chance of further tightening.
insights.quote: The Fed sees the US economy as healthy, with GDP growth of about 2.3% this year and an unemployment rate of just 4.1%.
insights.locator: The Fed sees the US economy as healthy

insights.claim: The full economic impact of 2026's oil price surge has not yet been felt and will continue playing out into next year and beyond, despite apparent near-term resilience in global growth.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Do not extrapolate current macro resilience; position for lagged demand destruction and margin compression in 2027.
insights.quote: Its analysis is a reminder that the full impact of the rise in oil prices this year has not yet been felt.
insights.locator: Its analysis is a reminder

themes.theme: Fuel price shock and the diesel squeeze

insights.claim: Brent crude rose from about US$60 a barrel at the start of January to about US$101 a barrel by mid-September 2026, yet global growth has remained generally stable so far.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A 68% crude move with no visible growth damage means the transmission lag, not immunity — watch 2027 consensus GDP revisions.
insights.quote: Global growth remains generally stable, despite Brent rising from about US$60 a barrel at the beginning of January to about US$101 a barrel on Monday morning.
insights.locator: Some commentators have observed

insights.claim: US average retail gasoline has reached about US$4.48 a gallon, up roughly 40% year on year, according to AAA data.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A 40% pump-price rise is a direct hit to discretionary consumer spend — negative for low-income retail, positive for refiner cracks.
insights.quote: The average retail price of gasoline in the US has risen to about US$4.48 a gallon, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), up about 40% from its level a year ago.
insights.locator: The average retail price of gasoline

insights.claim: US retail diesel averages about US$6.51 a gallon, up 76% over the past year, with Russia's ban on diesel exports a contributing cause of global market tightness.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Diesel, not gasoline, is the binding constraint — trade distillate cracks and freight-cost-exposed shippers and agriculture.
insights.quote: Diesel is currently retailing in the US at an average of about US$6.51 a gallon, up 76% over the past year.
insights.locator: The rise in diesel prices has been even sharper

insights.claim: At current price levels, the US's roughly 45 billion gallons of annual transport diesel consumption implies about US$125 billion of additional cost over a year, equal to about 0.4% of US GDP.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A quantified 0.4%-of-GDP tax on the economy — a reusable way to size the drag if diesel stays bid, concentrated in agriculture and fishing.
insights.quote: If prices stay at these levels for a year, that represents an additional cost of about US$125 billion, or about 0.4% of US GDP.
insights.locator: The US uses about 45 billion gallons

insights.claim: A shutdown at ExxonMobil's Joliet refinery in Illinois, originally triggered by a power outage, has added to the tightness of US diesel markets.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Idiosyncratic US refining outages are stacking on a tight global distillate balance — watch Midwest diesel differentials for restart timing.
insights.locator: A shutdown at ExxonMobil’s Joliet refinery

themes.theme: Policy response risk: the diesel export ban

insights.claim: Senator Chuck Grassley, representing agriculture-dependent Iowa, has urged President Trump to impose an embargo on US diesel exports, arguing high diesel prices are killing farmers' income.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Political pressure for export restrictions is now explicit; an actual ban would be a tail risk repricing US refiners and global distillate flows.
insights.quote: Over the weekend Senator Chuck Grassley, a Republican who represents the agriculture-dependent state of Iowa, urged President Donald Trump to put an embargo on US diesel exports.
insights.locator: Calls for an urgent policy response

insights.claim: Forcing US refineries to sell only domestically would make them cut crude runs by about 4 million b/d, reducing gasoline supply by about 1.8 million b/d and forcing the US to import more, driving consumer prices up rather than down.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: An export ban is a self-defeating policy — if it is announced, fade the initial bearish crack reaction and expect gasoline strength.
insights.quote: if US refineries were forced to sell only to the domestic market, they would have to cut crude runs by about 4 million b/d. As a result, gasoline supply would be reduced by about 1.8 million b/d
insights.locator: Jamie Lewis, Wood Mackenzie’s principal analyst

insights.claim: Superficially appealing export bans cannot solve high US fuel prices; only addressing the wider issues in world markets can, because US prices are set globally.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Discount headline relief measures — the structural fix requires Middle East de-escalation, so hedge accordingly.
insights.quote: Although an export ban might seem superficially appealing, a real solution to the problems facing the US as a result of higher fuel prices can come only from addressing the wider issues in world markets.

insights.claim: Germany's federal and state governments agreed a fuel price relief package including federal and state tax cuts plus talks with the oil industry on a proposed fuel price cap to be introduced by the beginning of 2027.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: European fiscal subsidisation of fuel props up demand and prolongs price pressure; a 2027 German price cap is a direct margin risk for downstream marketers there.
insights.quote: The package includes cuts in federal and state taxes, as well as a commitment to talks with the oil industry about a proposed fuel price cap, to be introduced by the beginning of 2027.
insights.locator: Lars Klingbeil, Germany’s finance minister

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's Macro Oils team forecasts world market tightness will drive Brent crude to US$125 per barrel in October if there is no agreement to resolve the Middle East conflict.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A dated, quantified house call roughly 24% above spot — an explicit directional bias for crude and energy equities into Q4.
insights.quote: Our Macro Oils team forecasts that the tightness of world markets will drive Brent crude to US$125 per barrel in October.
insights.locator: The Wood Mackenzie view

insights.claim: Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the country 'must both fight and negotiate' rather than choosing one, signalling no imminent de-escalation of the Middle East conflict.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Negotiation headlines should not be read as resolution — the geopolitical risk premium in crude is unlikely to bleed out quickly.
insights.quote: the country “must both fight and negotiate”, rather than opting for one or the other
insights.locator: The pressures that have driven prices higher

insights.claim: Ukraine struck the Moscow Oil Refinery with drones and Putin is reported to be planning further escalation including possible covert attacks in Europe, keeping Russian supply infrastructure under sustained attack.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Russian refining capacity is a live, repeatedly-hit target — reinforces the structural distillate deficit driving diesel cracks.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, Ukraine hit another Russian oil facility

insights.claim: Qatar's Pearl GTL complex, a supplier of base oil for premium lubricants, has been shut since being hit by an Iranian strike in March, and the resulting supply chain disruption pushed Costco to ration Kirkland Signature synthetic motor oil to 5 gallons per customer per week.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Conflict damage has already reached US retail shelves via specialty products — expect lubricant and base oil pricing power for unaffected producers.

themes.theme: AI capex as the macro single point of failure

insights.claim: Peter Martin, Wood Mackenzie's head of economics, estimates up to two-thirds of US GDP growth this year has been driven by AI-related capital spending, while broader domestic investment has remained lacklustre.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: US growth is a single-factor trade on AI capex; any hyperscaler capex guidance cut is effectively a macro downgrade.
insights.quote: Peter Martin, Wood Mackenzie’s head of economics, estimates that up to two-thirds of US GDP growth this year has been driven by AI-related capital spending.
insights.locator: From an economic point of view

insights.claim: The primary economic concern from higher oil prices is not direct fuel cost but the vulnerability of investor sentiment and the AI infrastructure boom to a higher interest rate environment.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: The oil-to-equities transmission channel runs through discount rates on long-duration AI capex, not through consumer gasoline spend.
insights.quote: our primary concern is the vulnerability of investor sentiment and the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom in an environment of higher interest rates
insights.locator: From an economic point of view

insights.claim: An end to the AI investment boom, combined with the squeeze on American consumers from higher fuel costs, could tip the US economy into recession.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: The recession path is explicitly two-factor — monitor AI capex announcements and retail fuel prices together as a joint recession indicator.
insights.quote: an end to the AI investment boom, added to the squeeze on American consumers from higher fuel costs, could tip the US economy into recession
insights.locator: Wood Mackenzie’s Martin said

insights.claim: Some leaders of the AI industry are themselves calling for a slowdown in the pace of development, adding an endogenous risk to the capex boom alongside rising short- and long-term interest rates.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Deflation of the boom may come from inside the industry, not just from financing costs — a risk not priced into AI infrastructure names.
insights.locator: With short-term and long-term interest rates rising

insights.claim: About US$18 billion of loans tied to an Oracle-backed data centre project in New Mexico were trading at a significant discount to par, after local opposition including challenges to permits for a natural gas pipeline needed to feed the project's fuel cells.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Data centre credit is already marking down on permitting and community risk — a leading indicator to watch in AI infrastructure debt spreads.
insights.quote: about US$18 billion of loans tied to a data centre project in New Mexico, which is backed by Oracle, were trading at a significant discount to par value
insights.locator: Widespread public resistance to data centre development

insights.claim: Widespread public resistance to data centre development is emerging as a distinct constraint on the AI industry's growth, separate from capital and chip availability.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Permitting and social licence, not just power and silicon, become the binding constraint — favours developers with secured sites and grid interconnects.
insights.locator: Widespread public resistance to data centre development

insights.claim: Google, Nvidia and Emerald AI have launched the AI Energy Management Alliance with 18 other energy and tech companies to promote flexible data centre loads as grid resources and prioritise speed-to-power for AI data centres.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Demand-response-capable data centres are becoming a lobbying priority — watch for grid-flexibility software and interconnection reform beneficiaries.

insights.claim: Continental Resources has signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Venezuela's PDVSA to operate and develop the Ayacucho 2 Block in the Orinoco Oil Belt, which Wood Mackenzie analysis puts at 7.4 billion barrels of recoverable heavy oil with no wells currently producing.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Privately held US producers are taking first-mover geopolitical risk in Venezuela; a large resource with zero production means very long-dated, optionality-style exposure.
insights.quote: Wood Mackenzie analysis indicates that Ayacucho 2 holds 7.4 billion barrels of recoverable heavy oil, but none of the wells there are currently in production.
insights.locator: Continental Resources, the privately held oil and gas producer

insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Capital is rotating from US shale into Latin American unconventionals with trader partners — a signal on where operators see better returns.

insights.claim: Disruption to food production from what could be a record-breaking El Nino weather event is a further inflation and growth risk layered on top of the fuel price shock.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A second, uncorrelated inflation impulse — agricultural commodities could compound the Fed's pass-through problem.

insights.claim: Gas-fired power in India is well positioned to support a renewables-led grid through peaking and flexibility services, but its commercial role will remain limited without improvements in fuel availability, market-based gas pricing and mechanisms that value system flexibility.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Indian gas turbine and LNG import demand stays capped until market design changes — a pricing-reform trigger to watch before sizing exposure.
